narrative:
The model predicted a 60.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

Three pieces of information drove that decision, ranked by importance. First, your LSAT score of 46 was the strongest factor. Surprisingly, this score is well above the average of students who were accepted, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward you passing the exam. However, the other two key factors outweighed this positive signal.

Your class rank at the end of your third year was the second most influential detail. Being in the third decile is noticeably lower than the average of accepted students, and this pulled the prediction toward failure. Similarly, your first-year class rank in the third decile, also below the typical rank of accepted applicants, was the third most important factor and further increased the estimated risk of failing the bar.

Taken together, the model concluded that your relatively lower performance during law school created too high a risk of bar exam failure, despite your strong LSAT result. 

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and class ranking in the remaining part of your program. Raising your standing in future coursework could meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor. Consider seeking academic support or tutoring to help move into a higher decile.
